  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 4 ## From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca. 1150-1360 In Chapter 3, I traced the increasingly widespread association of mucus with Wind disorders from the tenth to the twelfth century and showed that several illnesses whose pathomechanisms had been considered close to those of kuang—Wind strokes and xian 痈 seizures—were often treated with anti-mucus remedies by the end of that period. Let me now explain how the mucus-and-Fire etiology of madness that dominated late-imperial conceptions of insanity developed. The mucus-and-Fire script emerged among doctrinally minded physicians who lived in north China under the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), and was consolidated by southern doctors who were influenced by these northerners in the early fourteenth century under the Yuan dynasty (1260-1368), after the Mongol conquest of both the Jin and the southern Song (1127-1279) had re-established contacts between north and south China. The innovations these medical thinkers proposed built on the trends I outlined in Chapter 3, but it was their doctrinal and therapeutic precepts that came to dominate later medical thinking. During these men's lives (and partly thanks to their efforts), \"Cold Injury\" (shangban 傷寒) replaced \"Wind illnesses\" as the new dominant class of illnesses. The way Jin-Yuan physicians interpreted madness and handled mad people depended on their broader understanding of illness and vitality. The development of Cold- Injury medicine, for example, enhanced the importance of Heat and Fire as etiological factors and motivated a number of doctors to use Cold-Injury remedies to treat psycho- behavioral symptoms. Song Lian spoke of hundreds of disciples (“Epitaph”: 324), Xu’s biography in the History of the Yuan (189: 4320) of “more than one thousand.” Dongyang was a few kilometers east (upriver) of Yiwu, where Zhu lived. Like Zhu and Song, Xu Qian was from Wuzhou, an active Daoxue center in the fourteenth century (see Sun Kekuan 1975; John Langlois 1974 and 1981b; John Dardess 1982 and 1983; and Peter Bol 2001 and 2003).
Song Lian’s “Epitaph” (p. 324) mentioned that Zhu Zhenheng once “re-examined” (復考) the Family Rituals

Zhu had told his disciples that Shao’s teachings were at the foundation of medical learning. See Liu Chun 劉純, Yijing xiaoxue 醫經小學 (1388), “Yi zhe ke fa wei wen” 醫之可法為問 (LiuChYQ: 6). $ ^{118} $ Dai Liang 戴良 (1317-83), also a Wuzhou scholar, claimed that Zhu was well-versed in these two books (“Danxi weng zhuang” 丹溪翁傳 [“Biography of the Old Man of Danxi”; hereafter “Biography”]; Danxi yiji: 329). $ ^{119} $ Zhu quoted this text many times in “On Ministerial Fire” (“Xianghuo lun”相火論) (see below, pp. 117ff). $ ^{120} $ Song Lian (“Epitaph”: 324) indicated that Zhu took part in the provincial examinations (賓興) twice but failed both times (再往再不利). As an edition of the Jinhua prefectural gazetteer (“examinations”科第; cited in Danxi yijr: 704) recorded, only one candidate from Wuzhou passed the provincial examination in 1320. For more on the civil examinations under the Yuan dynasty, see Elman 2000: 30-38. $ ^{121} $ Dai Liang, “Biography”: 328. Xu’s biography in History of the Yuan (189: 4319) listed the “medical canons” (醫經) as one of the many types of books in which Xu was well versed.

recorded that Luo owned “thousands of books” (存書籍數千部), many of which must have been medical ones. For the date and English title of Kong Qi's work, I follow Smith 2003: 71. $ ^{138} $ Zhu’s preface to Gezhi yulun 格致餘論 claimed that Luo had also shown him books by Wang Haogu. $ ^{139} $ This passage alluded to physician Chunyu Yi’s biography in Shiji 105. As Chunyu’s master had purportedly told him: “dispose of all your recipe books: they are wrong” (盡去而方書 非是也). $ ^{140} $ Song Lian, “Epitaph”: 326. Huan 漁 usually meant water dissipating, but huan yan 漁焉 could refer more metaphorically to the dissipation of doubts (the second meaning of huan ran 漁然 in Hanyu da cidian, Suoyin ben: 3265C). Ningzhi 凝滯 referred to something congealed or blocked, in this case in the chest because this was where cognitive activities were thought to take place.
